name: David Graeber
summary: Graeber was an anthropologist and anarchist who argued for stateless, horizontally organised, consensus-based politics, direct action in place of electoral politics, and the cancellation of debt. He criticised capitalism, bureaucracy and pointless work, and backed a shorter working week and basic income.

sovereign-debt-cancellation.rationale: He says the movement’s long-term aim on Third World debt was an amnesty along the lines of the biblical Jubilee, and argues debts need not be repaid (Debt, opening chapter; Fragments).

open-borders.rationale: His three-point programme includes eliminating all restrictions on global freedom of travel or residence, and he says anarchism aims at eliminating national borders (Fragments).

abolish-ip.rationale: He proposes immediate cancellation of all patents and IP rights on technology more than a year old; this is a sweeping cut but not total abolition (Fragments).

direct-action.rationale: He describes anarchist politics as rejecting appeals to governments in favour of direct physical intervention against state power, and works through direct action networks (The New Anarchists).

means-match-ends.rationale: He endorses prefigurative politics: the organisational form of an activist group should embody the society it wants to create (The Democracy Project).

political-decisions-consensus.rationale: He describes consensus process as the anarchist way to decide, working proposals until everyone can live with them, and defends it against voting (Fragments; Twilight of Vanguardism).

participatory-democracy.rationale: He champions direct, horizontal democracy such as the general assemblies of Occupy as the way people should shape decisions (The Democracy Project).

vanguard-party.rationale: He argues anarchists reject vanguard parties and that leadership by a disciplined revolutionary elite is the model to leave behind (Twilight of Vanguardism).

basic-income.rationale: He names unconditional Universal Basic Income as the one current proposal that would shrink government intrusion and advocates it as a way out of the problems of Bullshit Jobs (conclusion).

job-guarantee.rationale: In Bullshit Jobs he argues guaranteed-jobs programmes are not improved versions of UBI and would not reduce government intrusion, so he prefers UBI instead.

limit-growth.rationale: He says the most pressing need is to slow down the engines of productivity because debt and climate change are driven by ever-rising output (A Practical Utopian’s Guide).

student-debt-relief.rationale: He calls for planetary debt cancellation as broad as practically possible, and says an amnesty on personal debt is worth considering (A Practical Utopian’s Guide; Fragments).

revolution-legitimate.rationale: He treats revolution as a legitimate and still-living project, defining it as planetwide transformations of political common sense and urging movements to pursue the end of capitalism and the state (A Practical Utopian’s Guide; Revolutions in Reverse).

automate-paid-work.rationale: He argues technological development should be redirected toward eliminating disciplined, pointless labour entirely and proposes a four-hour day (A Practical Utopian’s Guide; Finance interview).

state-harmful.rationale: As an anarchist he argues for a society without states, saying nation-states’ effacement is true globalization and that governments are not needed to keep order (Fragments; Are You an Anarchist?).

abolish-police-prisons.rationale: He says the anti-social behaviour used to justify police, prisons and armies is caused by the inequalities they uphold, and cites places where police vanished without chaos (Are You an Anarchist?; Freedom and Anarchy interview).

abolish-armed-forces.rationale: He says anarchists want a society where top-down military organisations such as armies are no longer necessary, though he frames it as a long-run possibility (Are You an Anarchist?).

political-elite-corrupt.rationale: He says power corrupts and that those who spend their lives seeking it are the last who should hold it, and treats the view that politicians are selfish as a broadly shared anarchist premise (Are You an Anarchist?).

patriarchy-structural.rationale: He lists male dominance with the state, capitalism and racism as institutions that are not inevitable and could be replaced (Fragments); this treats them as structures of domination, though he does not elaborate the claim there.

workplace-democracy.rationale: He sets out workers’ control, the principle that anyone engaged in a project has an equal say in it, as one of the two pillars of radical democratic thought and discusses it as the basis for a democratic workplace (The Democracy Project).

work-for-welfare.rationale: He backs unconditional basic income and says conditional benefit or guaranteed-job versions are not variants of it and add government intrusion (Bullshit Jobs, conclusion).

targeted-social-spending.rationale: He favours replacing means-tested welfare with a flat payment to everyone and calls the means-testing apparatus the problem (Bullshit Jobs, conclusion).

legal-duty-to-work.rationale: He says labour discipline is a misfortune that is at best sometimes necessary, rejects the idea that work is virtuous in itself, and backs an unconditional income (A Practical Utopian’s Guide; Bullshit Jobs).

work-centre-of-life.rationale: He argues the real business of human life is mutual care, not contributing to “the economy”, and that labour is virtuous only when it helps others (A Practical Utopian’s Guide).

one-party-rule.rationale: He calls for a self-consciously non-vanguardist politics and says the vanguard model that gave one party the lead has run its course (The Twilight of Vanguardism).

dictatorship-of-proletariat.rationale: He says revolutionaries who imposed their visions through a machinery of violence were wrong, and that freedom cannot be advanced by creating new forms of coercion (Fragments).

strong-leader.rationale: He holds that people cannot be trusted with power over others and that power corrupts, so those who seek it should be the last to hold it (Are You an Anarchist?).

natural-rulers.rationale: He rejects the belief that some kinds of people are destined to be ruled by their betters and says people can organise themselves without being told how (Are You an Anarchist?).

sovereign-above-law.rationale: He argues that power corrupts and that anyone given power over others will almost invariably abuse it (Are You an Anarchist?).

democracy-is-procedure.rationale: He argues that elections were historically seen as the aristocratic way to choose officials and that Americans mean something far broader than voting by democracy (The Democracy Project).

offices-by-lottery.rationale: He presents lottery (sortition) as the genuinely democratic way of filling office, because elections are an aristocratic mode that breeds factionalism, though he does not campaign for it outright (The Democracy Project).

decide-locally.rationale: He says anarchists would put as much power as possible in small communities while allowing that some coordination is still needed (Are You an Anarchist?).

corporate-influence.rationale: He writes that a bank’s lobbying spend went directly to the politicians who wrote the tax codes letting it pay nothing, and describes finance and government colluding against citizens (The Democracy Project).

consumerism-harmful.rationale: He says anarchists wanted fewer working hours rather than the consumer utopia of infinite growth, and wants technology steered away from ever more consumer products (Against Kamikaze Capitalism; A Practical Utopian’s Guide).

refuse-lender-austerity.rationale: He argues IMF structural-adjustment conditions did direct damage, were imposed without citizens’ consent and did not work, and that he and fellow activists wanted to stop them (Debt, opening chapter).

world-economy-extracts-surplus.rationale: He says thirty years of money flowing from the poorest countries to the richest was quite enough, treating that flow as the core harm of Third World debt (Debt, opening chapter).

universal-healthcare.rationale: He calls the European social welfare state, with its free education and universal health care, one of the greatest achievements of human civilization, while criticising its bureaucratic, top-down form (The Utopia of Rules).

unions-good.rationale: He lists the gutting of union power and the destruction of unions through precarious work among the ways elites depoliticised labour, and notes that the welfare institutions of Europe came from unions and cooperatives (Bullshit Jobs; A Practical Utopian’s Guide; The Utopia of Rules).

worker-ownership.rationale: Speaking as the anarchist in his dialogue, he names worker self-management such as Mondragon among the successful experiments, and he describes occupied factories as experiments in mutual aid (Fragments; Revolutions in Reverse).

markets-allocate-better.rationale: He argues that the “free market” ideology is a political project that is the opposite of what it claims, that a market economy needs vast bureaucracy, and that capitalism generates pointless jobs rather than allocating labour well (Bullshit Jobs; The Utopia of Rules).

notes: Searched his books, essays and interviews by keyword for each theme (work, debt, state, police, unions, markets, regulation, taxes, health care, religion, war, intervention, race, gender, animals, technology, climate, Occupy). Where the texts only describe a view or discuss a topic without him taking a position, the answer is null. Debt amnesty and anti-austerity answers come from Debt; the Wikipedia article (s23) was used for orientation only.
